So it means nothing happened in ground with that issue, so it's more important for my purposes to review the reports of the brigade, of the people, what were doing on the ground. So order itself, it doesn't mean that this what is ordered really happened. So for how many days it would be enough to collect bodies from the area, I don't know. We don't have any indication that that happened. We don't have witnesses who would testify about that or who would give us a statement. And I would imagine if this happened on the terrain, many people would be involved. And all those years we would for sure get information from these people, what happened, what they were doing, and where did they bury these people, these bodies which were collected from the ground. And that's indication, you know, which is missing in the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, in your previous answer you said the graves we are talking about were opened and closed in very short period of time. I think last one is closed on the 7th of July. It's page 46, line 25 to page 47, line 2. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but if I said 7, it should be 17th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, 17th of July. What did you mean by being "closed"? And what evidence do you have in terms of the graves being closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is coming out from the aerial images where we can see that the soil is put over that -- that excavation was done at the grave-site, and I think that I'm getting information from the expert archaeologists, from their reports, saying the grave by that time was closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have evidence that was opened again and closed again in a short time? I meant to say that do you have evidence that excludes the fact that graves were opened and closed shortly after the initial burial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We have evidence from later on, two months later, when the reburials took place. And you can see the disturbances are, again, at the same spots where the primary graves were disposed. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you rely on rather the archaeologist and pathologist or anthropologist evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, and they did take the aerial images into consideration in their reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, by now you have spent the same amount of time as the Prosecution used in -- for their examination-in-chief. When I told you that it may be fair enough for you to use the whole session, I thought I was of the opinion that you would still have an hour left. But given the situation -- and I have the feeling that you can conclude in 20 minutes' time from now. Let us see how it evolves.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I would like to rely on Ms. West's estimate, that she'd need five minutes for her re-direct. So I'd like to avail myself of all that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also have in mind that the forthcoming two witnesses, whether we can finish them all by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best because this witness is an important witness, a very important witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, do you have any proof of that order being changed? Was another one issued replacing it?
I don't have any information right now in this regard. I don't even remember it from top of my head. I would need to take a look to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any proof of the technical services not carrying out the orders of a colonel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's not for the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant on the basis of what he was concluding, that perhaps that had not happened. But all right, let us see whether we agree that the aerial images show the period between the 7th and the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have aerial images from the 17th until the 27th of July taken on a daily basis?

No, we don't have them on a daily basis, for sure not. And I'm not quite sure how many of them we have. Because I know that we requested several times for more and more, and we were provided with additional aerial images, also for other areas, not only for these mass graves. So -- but to give you an exact answer, I would need to take a look to analyse them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the area of the Zvornik Brigade, did you get a single aerial image between the 17th and the 27th of July?
Same as before, I would need to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now of this document that we have before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see this in the third paragraph -- no, fourth paragraph, roughly ten dead and 20 wounded persons. Some of those who got killed and wounded were soldiers carrying weapons, and then a bit further down it says that a group of 200 to 300 people split in two. And then we see that 50 people were hiding in the grass.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the next page where it says that they killed three of their own, believing that they were Chetniks. No one believed them. One of them was shouting and saying, "I'm a Muslim, I'm a Muslim," and nobody believed him. They shot them. And then a Muslim unit confirmed that indeed these had been their people, and then there's a reference to 30 bodies in the fourth line, and then towards the bottom of the last page he saw a man who tried to commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the third paragraph, ten people who did not wish to surrender committed suicide. I saw them lie down and put hand-grenades under their stomachs. They blew themselves up. From the statements of persons who managed to get through in the column, did you take into account all of these losses? Did you locate the places of death and the places where they were buried?

For some of them, yes, it's true, but not for all of them. And one of those examples is the witness who testified here in January, and I was going over this issue about the bodies being seen by him as being killed and they were found on the surface. So I can run a search for these people right now if you want, and we can check where they would appear, if these are the ones he saw they were killed because he was, I think, talking - this witness we have in front of us - was talking in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness says that three Muslims were killed by the Muslims themselves because there was this confusion. They believed that they were Serbs. Then ten committed suicide. Also he says that 30 were killed in combat, so that is 43 at least. Did you get the names of these persons from him or at least the names of those who he had known?

I'm sure investigators asked him about the names during the interview, and if he listed those names they would appear here. Like if we go down to the last paragraph, he names the people who surrendered. It's just the fact that the people, they don't know sometimes everybody and that's why they were not -- they were unable to provide any names. And it's many of those statements in OTP records, and I can say that I haven't reviewed all of them systematically in a way to extract the individuals from these statements and to compare them against the ICMP list. But whenever I did that, my conclusions and the ICMP identifications were corroborated. So it fit the story of the survivors or witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have these conclusions of yours, this material that includes the names that you received from the witness and then collated?

Yes, I know that the biggest such analysis was done in preparation within the OTP to submit the Popovic final brief. At that point in time I was engaged in checking the names which were listed by different survivors, different witnesses, who testified in that case. And I was corroborating or trying to find where they were found. And there is such list. I don't know in what shape it was produced within the final brief. I don't have it with me right now, but I think it's traceable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How do you know they were not buried? How do you know that they were surface remains? These persons that this man had seen with his very own eyes, 43 dead at least?

It's always difficult to establish if you don't have names, you know. You have to have name in order to establish where certain individual was found or buried. I mean, instances - and there is many of such statements like this one where people would say, Yes, I saw many of them being killed in ambush, and they don't list any names, it's always difficult to prove who those people are and where they are found.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if they were buried during the sanitisation process, are they added to the number of persons who were executed? Look at page number 2 -- and then from there onwards he sees 30 bodies, a few persons killed this way or that way, so none of that is in Pobudje. It's in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. Where were they buried?

You know, we see that we have in Baljkovica area, we have at least 60 surface remains. Perhaps those are the ones or some of the ones are the ones. So I don't know because I don't have name. If we speculate. For example, further, you know, like you say that they would end up in mass grave, yes, if this is the case, if this can be proven, if we can find one -- one individual which was actually on -- killed and named by one of those survivors and he ended up in mass grave, that person would appear in my report as being found in the mass grave. So -- but first we have to establish. So far we haven't. Whenever I've checked and cross-checked different names, they fit the story of the survivors. For example, one saw the killing in Pobudje area, named these people, and I found to be still there. One, for example, witnesses the execution. And yes, it was corroborated the people who he named were executed there or were found in mass grave. So it's always important you have names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, I believe that the Defence is in a better position from that point of view. You have to prove that rather than say that all of those who are in mass graves had been executed. And now let the Defence make an effort and disprove that. You have to prove that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, Excellencies, you do not admit such statements, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, we will not admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D5492, could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We moved already, but, Mr. Robinson, what was the reason why we shouldn't have broadcast the previous document, the witness statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know of any, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I don't know of any either. Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: He's about to use another statement. We will check right now as to whether it should be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this to be public, but I wanted to allow the Prosecution to say whether it had to be confidential or not. Let's now have a look at page 3 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the third paragraph can you see that it says that there were about 15.000 of them in total? And then we'll scroll down a bit, and in the fourth paragraph it says that fire was opened and that at that location on a hill they arrived at, about 500 people were killed. Did you question this witness to find out the names of the people that he was with? One should assume that he knew at least some of them?
Personally me, I did not. But maybe it comes out from the statement itself, what did he say or if he asked -- he was asked this question, if he listed any of those people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's scroll further down -- in fact, can we see the next page. In the fourth paragraph 2.000 people are referred to, mixed civilians and soldiers. And in paragraph 5 it says there I found about 50 bodies. So that's quite different from the first site. It says some still of them alive. The Serbs had stabbed them with knives in the stomach and so on. So in total that is over 500. Can we have a look at the next page. Five or killed in a minefield. Can we have a look at the next page, at the end of this largest paragraph, paragraph 3. Five were killed in a minefield, two survived, Kadir and Huso, and so on. This person mentioned several hundred people whom he saw and who he saw were killed. Did your team manage to identify the people concerned and did your team exclude them from the ICMP list? Did they determine where they were buried? Did your team determine what their names were? Was anything established in relation to these victims?

I'm not aware of any such analysis being done regarding this, but when we are talking about statements like this one, when witnesses have been referring to certain amount of people being killed, we have to be very conservative as to their figures because it's not very easy to assess, especially under conditions they were under, to assess how many people would in reality be killed or how many people they observed at certain location. I know from my experience as a professional, as a police officer, there is a special training provided for police officers to assess how many people is gathered at the same place, even with that -- with their training people will do mistakes. So we have to be careful with the numbers, but to, yeah, answer your question, I don't have any knowledge of this analysis being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But in criminal legal affairs you agree that when we're dealing with unlawful killings, such matters should be matters that are determined beyond any reasonable doubt?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Also not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness is a policeman who was involved in investigations. So I don't see why this question is not appropriate. Let's have a look at 1D5491.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this letter? It's an exchange between the Government of Republika Srpska and Mr. Masovic. The next document is his response. Were you familiar with this?
I'm not sure that I'm familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a look at the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what Masovic said in response to this request made by Mr. Spaic. Mr. Spaic requested this be provided and this is what Amor Masovic says. He says the institute has information - it's in 2008 - the institute has information about 3.214 identified victims of genocide buried in the Memorial Complex and 168 identified victims buried in several local graveyards. And then it says -- let's see what it says in English. [In English] "We also have information that the DNA laboratory in Tuzla has completed the preliminary identification of about 2.000 other victims that have still not been identified by their next of kin." [Interpretation] So 3.200 were identified on the basis of DNA and on the basis of family members, and 2.000 others were identified on the basis of DNA analysis but they hadn't been identified by their family members. Were you aware of the fact that that was the situation in 2008?

I think I was and I think it should be still the same situation. Perhaps the numbers would be different now, much more of them identified and buried than only waiting for final identification, but that's the process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 63 you said that in Cerska twins were found. Were they identified and were they being searched for?

I didn't say that in Cerska grave were -- the twins were found, but I was testifying about is that we most probably have the twins, one found in Cerska grave, the other in one of the Hodzici grave, but we have only one identification. It's always difficult for the ICMP to identify such cases because only one DNA sample would be retrieved. So that DNA sample would apply for both brothers, for both twins. In such situations there is only anthropological way of distinguishing the two. And that's what is actually done. The process, when it's done -- the identification done by the ICMP, it's not the final step. They sent their findings back to the pathologists, who are then making the final determination of the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 70 you confirmed that in relation to Mr. Parsons you confirmed that there was a certain amount of confusion, disorder, in the graves. And you clarified the confusion in favour of the Prosecution's claim. Don't you think this was somewhat difficult challenge?

No, it was not a challenge at all, and it was not in a Prosecution favour. I was just trying in a way to defend my report, to find -- to present that what was stated here by Mr. Parsons, it's not entirely true. For example, because he wasn't aware exactly where such individuals were found because he hasn't examined those site codes in such detail, which was done by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were shown a list and -- in fact, did you notice that the same names and surnames appear in our area. We're not very imaginative when it comes to giving names, the same names are often used.
Yes, that's what I came across, even you would have situations where you have first and last name the same, also father's name would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 71 to page 72, Ms. West showed you the name of a certain Nusret whose little daughter was the subject of testimony. Was it confirmed for certain that that was that Nusret?

I would say most certainly it is because it has the first and last name the same, father's name the same. I found two individuals with first and last name and father's name the same, but the difference was the date of birth. One was born in 1966 and the other one in 1954. The one which was 1966 would fit the description from that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it wasn't determined for sure that it was, in fact, that person?

For fact, in order for me to confirm it for fact, I would rather consult some other sources as well, for example, date of birth and place of birth and perhaps their family members. This can be done through demographic data we have the OTP available. So it very often happened in this case and also when I was part of the investigation team that I would come across such situation. I was unable to say who that person is or to confirm, yes, this is the person. In such cases I would consult those sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On pages 77 to 79 Himza was mentioned who was wounded. Apart from using the bandages as an indication, was it established in some other way that the very same Himza was, in fact, concerned?

Yes. In this particular case I did check all individuals with the same first and last name being born or lived in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. I think I found three of them, and I was able to exclude one definitely because he was not the victim or he didn't die. The second one I think is found -- is a victim of this Srebrenica event as well but found somewhere -- in some different location. What I did was I consulted their place of birth and family members, and I concluded that this is Himza Mujic they were talking about, the one found in Bisina grave, because he was from the area of Han Pijesak where the police officer Jovovic, who we interviewed, was also coming from. This same Himza Mujic was having this bandage and he was in prison, and also taken into consideration that the killing took place on 23rd of July and intercept reflects - which is the day after - that he left recently and that Popovic would know where he was, so would indicate that he disappeared and he was not in the prison on 24th anymore. So all those little pieces which I could get from different documents and records, I would put it together, and doing that I was able to establish that, yes, this is Himzo Mujic in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned mitochondrial in relation to DNA. This was a different sample what the ICMP did. Is this the same thing or is it a different procedure? Any differences? Are these procedures compatible?

No, they are different. And I will just say the basics, what I know as a police officer. You have two different analysis, DNA analysis mitochondrial and nuclear. Nuclear is more precise. Mitochondrial, what you will get, it's -- we are all getting mitochondrial DNA from mother. It would be -- every single child would get the same mitochondrial DNA because we are getting it from mother. So for such identifications like ICMP is doing, it's useless -- but for some other aspects of investigation, it can be useful, for example, just to eliminate certain people as being related to one family. So you can't exclude -- but these are different methods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I just have another three brief questions. We agreed, or rather, you said that the Cerska grave hadn't been disturbed. If we were to find someone in it who had been captured on the 17th of July, that means no killing took place on the 13th; isn't that correct?
Yes, it's most probably the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take DNA samples from the Serbs? Is there a database for Serbian DNA? Did you get involved in such things?

Not me personally, but I assume the ICMP did get involved in this process as well because they are making identifications for all the missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Serbs, Muslims, from all the sides. So I would assume they have these samples from Serbs as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some Serbs still being searched for?
I don't know for the exact figure, but I'm sure that not everybody were found so far. There are many, many still on the missing list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the ICMP include in its list remains that had a DNA profile but remains that hadn't been associated with a given individual or with a given family?

No, this would not appear on their list, but it is somewhere in their database. They have DNA profiles for individuals which are not attached to any family members and those we are calling - and I present in my report - as unique, unmatched DNA profiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you say that they were killed on the basis of the information according to which they were found in mass graves, although we don't have any names and know nothing else about them apart from the fact that we have their DNA profiles and we know about the sites where they were found?
So just to give you a short answer, yes, and I think I explained once already during these procedures why.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. If I had more time I'd put more questions to you, but I think we have covered most of the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just want to put on the record a misstatement -- I want to put on the record a correction to an earlier misstatement made by Mr. Karadzic. On page 20 of today's transcript, in speaking about the date of execution at Cerska, he said this is the first time this Defence is hearing this and this is the first time that the Trial Chamber is hearing that perhaps the execution at Cerska did not happen at the 13th. I want to point out to the Trial Chamber in our pre-trial at paragraph 241 is our -- the Prosecution's allegation that at some point between the 13th and the 17th of July the VRS and MUP forces participated in the execution of Cerska Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the indictment says on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm just pointing out that this is not the first time that this has been suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, earlier today -- earlier today in cross-examination you were asked about some of the columns in the ICMP database, particularly place of disappearance and time of disappearance. And there had been a discussion between the difference of the ICMP information versus the ICRC information. Do you remember that discussion?
I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And particularly at page 12 today, in talking about the ICMP mandate or purpose, you said in the interviews with the families they were trying to get blood sample. Is it true that the main purpose of that ICMP interview was to get that DNA sample, that blood sample?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just under some time constraints here and I'm trying to push it along.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What was the main purpose of the ICMP interview?
To get these DNA samples from the relatives of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when did the ICMP first start those interviews?

I know they commenced its work in 2001. When they started actual process of getting DNA samples from the relatives, I'm not sure of, was it the same year, subsequent years, so I would need to check that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But at least it's after 2001?
Yes, that's my understanding. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during that period of -- during those interviews when they were taking the blood sample, is it your understanding that they also asked some questions of these people?
Yes, they have to. And I'm aware that they asked certain questions, but I don't have questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. Mr. Janc, could the lapse in time from the actual events in 1995 to the date of the interview in 2001 affect the reliability of the information that they gave to ICMP, the verbal information they gave to ICMP?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speculation. Speculation is being sought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you leave it -- we can leave it, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, at page 10 today you were asked how the IC [sic] got its information, and your answer was: "From relatives at the time when reported after the fall." Can you tell us when the ICRC began interviewing people in regard to the events of July 1995? Was it at the time or was it later?
I'm not sure about the exact date. I think I saw the first list being compiled or titled as -- or dated as 1996. But I think they were conducting this already before.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And so in -- we're speaking specifically about the issue -- the column of place of disappearance and time of disappearance. And you have told this Chamber that you found the ICRC list more reliable than the ICMP list. Can you tell the Chamber why?

Basically because there is more information and you can see the differences between this information, and it will point you at more accurate information as to when certain individuals might disappear. But I have to emphasize here also that also this data within the ICRC list are not very accurate for some of the individuals, because I did find discrepancies within those data, comparing, for example, when certain person might disappear and where it was later found. So I would not rely 100 per cent on those data either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you going to deal with Dean Manning --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- report or shall I leave it to the -- yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That was the last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, in follow-up to His Honour's questions from yesterday, you'll remember this discussion about the 35 people and then your footnote which referred to the Dean Manning report. Have you had an opportunity to look at this?
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about the numbers, the 35 and the 44 and the 45?

Yes, there is mistake but it does not affect the total numbers. So it should be noted - and I'm referring now to page 2 of my report, footnote number 4 - I would say 45 individuals were identified in total, so 45 can be found on this Manning list. And out of that, ten of them were included into the ICMP update. So it means again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So 9 in footnote 4 should read 10?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, number 44 should read 45, and number 9 should read 10. So -- and it will -- brings us again to 35 in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I would -- reviewing that, I spotted another little mistake in my report. If you go to -- in relation to the same issue, to Branjevo Military Farm grave. The same, it doesn't change the totals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The page is annex A, page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So you see, I have 127 individuals identified by the ICMP and 11 individuals identified by -- before. So it is actually 126 individuals identified by the ICMP and 12 individuals identified by before. Annex D is correct. You will find all the names there, but just this is a small difference, and it doesn't affect any totals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the record, please, may I say the following. I did not have time to shed more light on the witness's statement in relation to the six persons from 645. However, I will have an opportunity to do so because I still claim that things are the way I had put them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Six persons from 645. I don't think I followed your question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 045, Witness 045 confirmed that he saw six persons as they were being killed -- or rather, two went missing. But the witness tried to challenge that. However, I don't have time to deal with it. Your Excellency, you said "maybe Karadzic will deal with this."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have dealt with it without asking unnecessary or improper questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Janc, that concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question from me is that whether it was your idea to think about the DNA connections between the graves or is it somebody else's idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's my idea, and I started it first in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to thank you on behalf of this Chamber for you -- for your evidence and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We all rise all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We are a little bit late. I wanted to raise one matter quickly in private session, but I'll leave that to the Court. It really is a 30-second matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move -- but shall we deal with it in the absence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think since it is in private session we probably need to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, you may be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, shall we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. With the kind indulgence of the interpreters and the staff, we decided to reduce the time for the break to 45 minutes, so we'll resume at 1.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I was told that we'll resume in closed session. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
